title: Nitzavim: all of you (Deuteronomy 29:9–10)
hook: everyone stands in the covenant, leaders and woodcutters and water-drawers alike

segments.voice: Yesterday, a heart to know, given only after forty years. Your line was understanding takes years. What did you let be not yet? Today, a new portion, and a crowd. Day five hundred seventeen.

At any big gathering, a wedding, a graduation, a funeral, someone is at the front. Someone has the good seats. And someone is out back, in the kitchen, clearing plates, parking cars, carrying folding chairs. Nobody photographs them. Without them the day doesn't happen. The portion called Nitzavim opens with a crowd like that, and it does something unusual. It names the people in the kitchen. Not as an afterthought, and not at the edge. In the same sentence as the leaders.
screen: `THE FRONT, THE GOOD SEATS.` → `THE KITCHEN, THE PARKING LOT.` → `NAMED IN THE SAME SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Nitzavim means standing, standing firm. The portion opens: "Ye are standing this day all of you before the LORD your God: your heads, your tribes, your elders, and your officers, even all the men of Israel." Then the list keeps going: the little ones, the wives, the stranger in the camp, "from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water." That's the whole society, top to bottom. All of you. In an ancient camp, cutting wood and hauling water were the heaviest, lowest-status jobs. The people who did them didn't make decisions. They made the fire and the water possible. And here they stand in the covenant, named, no lower in the sentence's dignity than anyone else. Rashi, following a midrash, says these woodcutters and water-drawers were people from outside who had come to join Israel. If so, the circle is wider still: newcomers stand in the covenant too. It matters when this portion is read. In most years it falls on the Shabbat just before Rosh Hashanah, when people think about standing before God in judgment. The text answers ahead of time: you won't stand alone, and you won't stand ranked. Everyone stands. In many synagogues, the people who set out chairs, cook for the meal afterward, and lock up at night are the reason anyone else can be there at all. Nitzavim gives them their own line.
screen: `NITZAVIM: STANDING.` · `HEADS, ELDERS, OFFICERS.` · `THE HEWER OF WOOD, THE DRAWER OF WATER.` · `EVERYONE STANDS, UNRANKED.` · then, large: `ALL OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: value one role people overlook. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you spend time: work, school, a building, a congregation, your own home. Who makes it work without being seen? The cleaner, the night guard, the person who restocks the shelves, the one who always notices when the dish soap runs out. See their face if you can. Let them stand, in your mind, in the same line as the people at the front. Then think of one small way to tell them you've noticed. The bell holds the time.
Nitzavim. Standing. The portion where everyone stands together, from the heads of the tribes to the drawer of water.
Your line: all of you. Today, thank one person whose work usually goes unseen, by name if you can. Day five hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Nitzavim is usually read on the Shabbat before Rosh Hashanah, and its opening words, 'you are standing this day, all of you', are often taken up in sermons for the High Holy Days.

myth: only the leaders stood in the covenant
the list runs from heads and elders to children, strangers and water-drawers.

fork.setup: you're Moses, listing who stands in the covenant. you've named the heads, the elders and the officers. who comes next?
options: no one else: leaders speak for everyone.
children, wives, strangers, woodcutters and water-drawers.
fork.reveal: the list runs all the way down the camp, from the heads of the tribes to the drawer of water.

original.note: Hebrew: standing, standing firm. the key word of Deuteronomy 29:9 and the name of the portion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a crowd scene.
what it means: the covenant includes everyone, from leaders to the lowest-status workers and newcomers.
what a scholar hears: 'hewers of wood and drawers of water' returns in Joshua 9 with the Gibeonites; Rashi reads the phrase here as outsiders who came to join Israel.

notes: Deuteronomy 29:9–10 (JPS numbering; 29:10–11 in Christian Bibles) quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Rashi on 29:10 says these were Canaanites who came to convert in Moses' day (cf. the Gibeonites in Joshua 9); the script softens this to 'people from outside who had come to join Israel'. Keeper may wish to adjust.
Nitzavim is read on the Shabbat before Rosh Hashanah in most years (sometimes combined with Vayelech).
